sourceVerification.conditions: The general 2026–2027 route contains 60 EC compulsory study in Year 1; 45 EC compulsory study plus 15 EC constrained choices in Year 2; and 30 EC prescribed study plus 30 EC open academic study in Year 3. Academic Writing (3 EC), Computer Security (6 EC) and HCI (6 EC) are selected choices, not compulsory for everyone. There is no formal specialization. Object-Oriented and Functional Programming and Operating Systems require prior Computer Programming or Systems Programming Project; an approved earlier programming pair is also accepted for the former. Project entry requires at least 120 EC of the Computer Science bachelor. Students arrange a topic and supervisor before starting, normally in periods 5–6; a semester 1 project is possible through the coordinator. Internships require prior approval of a VU staff examiner. Projects may be individual or group work, with distinct student roles and individual assessment by two examiners: technical contribution 50%, thesis 40%, oral presentation 10%, each at least 5.5. The supervisor must submit the graded thesis and form by 31 July for August graduation or 31 January for February graduation. Generative AI is allowed for orientation and brainstorming, but cannot supply final-submission content. English diagnostic testing and the required refresher are mandatory without extra EC. BSA ordinarily requires 42 EC of first-year credits, subject to exceptions. Practical and tutorial attendance follows unit manuals; Smart Systems Engineering requires practical attendance and passing labs, with no practical resit. Thesis and placement regulations apply. Individual open choices need prior board approval, at least 12 EC at level 300 and at most 6 EC at level 100. Abroad, at most one 6 EC master unit may be included and cannot be reused later. Eligible university or listed minors can be taken without prior board approval. The general Data Science and Basics of AI university minors are excluded for CS students; the CS-specific Business Analytics and Data Science minor remains eligible. Optional minors are not stacked.

courseReview.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseReview.content: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courseReview.contribution: Mandatory Year1PPD; excluded from nonPPD trace requirement.

courseReview.name: Consumer Product Design
courseReview.content: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
courseReview.contribution: Contributes customer-needs interviews, product-concept formulation, quantitative modelling, prototyping, team planning and sustainability decisions as complementary design practice. It is a physical consumer-product course, not software requirements engineering or HCI.

courseReview.name: AI Ethics
courseReview.content: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
courseReview.contribution: examines ethical issues in designing and deploying AI

courseReview.name: Decision-making in AI
courseReview.content: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
courseReview.contribution: Studies planning under uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints; this is algorithmic AI decision making, not generic human judgment.

courseReview.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
courseReview.content: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
courseReview.contribution: teaches logic and discrete mathematics for formal computer science

courseReview.name: Optimization Methods in AI
courseReview.content: Artificial Intelligence is concerned with building intelligent machines that can compute how to act effectively and safely in a wide variety of novel situations. Computer agents operate autonomously, perceive their environment, persist over a prolonged time period, adapt to change, and create and pursue goals. A rational agent is one that acts so as to achieve the best expected outcome. This course aims to provide the student with foundational abilities in: searching in complex and adversarial environment and optimizing by rational agents. Topics include uninformed and informed search in discrete and completely known environments, local and global search methods in unknown and continuous environments, games played in adversarial environments and constraint satisfaction problems. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of experimental investigations into areas such as graph search, constraint satisfaction, convex optimization, linear and non-linear programming. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
courseReview.contribution: studies mathematical optimization for computational problems

courseReview.name: Reinforcement Learning
courseReview.content: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.
courseReview.contribution: studies reinforcement learning algorithms

courseReview.name: Networks & Operating Systems
courseReview.content: Computer networks are the foundations on which the modern commercial, entertainment, industrial, and social world is built. An operating system (OS) is system software that is the interface between computer hardware and applications. The first part of the semester is organized around layers of a computer network architecture. The main focus is on the Internet, its architecture and protocols are used for studying fundamental concepts. The second half of the semester starts by introducing the typical structure of an OS, by distinguishing between processes and threads, and by explaining how an OS schedules work. Then consideration is given to the issues of concurrency, memory management, and file systems. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with how the Internet works and how the Internet can be monitored and controlled, moreover, a sound understanding of the pivotal role an OS plays in the managing of resources and the running of applications.
courseReview.contribution: studies computer networks and operating systems directly

courseReview.name: Database Management Systems
courseReview.content: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courseReview.contribution: develops relational database concepts and query systems

courseReview.name: Software Development
courseReview.content: Software development is designing, creating, testing, and maintaining software applications. We learn to program in C++, which offers fine-grained control over system resources, and in Haskell, which is a purely functional programming language. Various stages of software development such as planning and requirements gathering, testing and quality assurance, deployment and maintenance is covered in laboratory format consisting mostly on in-class discussions and code reviews. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of programming in C++ and in Haskell. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
courseReview.contribution: Directly develops software in C++ and Haskell, with requirements gathering, testing, code review and projects. Its specific object-oriented and functional programming is aligned with that VU subject; it does not certify the complete software-engineering curriculum.

courseReview.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
courseReview.content: This course aims to provide the student with knowledge, skills and critical thinking ability in algorithm design and analysis. Inappropriate choice of algorithm and associated data structure can seriously impact on the performance of an application. The st udy of algorithm design and analysis provides techniques which help minimize the execution time of an algorithm. An emphasis is on the experimental performance analysis of algorithms. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Larger algorithm projects are also undertaken. There is a written midterm exam and a written final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained an understanding of how algorithms have helped shape the modern world.
courseReview.contribution: develops algorithm and data structure design

courseReview.name: Advanced Algorithms
courseReview.content: The realm of Algorithms certainly needs further exploration beyond the standard topics of an Algorithms and Data Structures course. We study modern algebraic algorithms and solution methods for optimization problems. The course will provide you with the knowledge and experience of advanced computational techniques with emphasis on algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of experimental investigations into areas such as fast arithmetic, arbitrary precision and advanced optimization methods. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
courseReview.contribution: deepens algorithm analysis and design

courseReview.name: Introduction to Data Science
courseReview.content: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
courseReview.contribution: introduces data handling, analysis and visualization

courseReview.name: Machine Learning
courseReview.content: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
courseReview.contribution: introduces machine learning methods

courseReview.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
courseReview.content: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.
courseReview.contribution: applies computing to image data and computer vision

courseReview.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courseReview.content: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
courseReview.contribution: Studies neural-network theory and Python/TensorFlow implementations for tabular, vision and text classification; image generation is conditional on time, not promised.

courseReview.name: Robotics
courseReview.content: Robotics is a broad interdisciplinary field that integrates computing science, mathematics, various branches of engineering, and, more recently, also knowledge from social sciences and humanities. In addition to introducing the participants to key notions and concepts in robotics and industrial automation, the course focuses on computational problems that arise in the field, in particular related to motion and manipulation, which are core abilities of an autonomous robot. Among the main topics that we address is kinematics, which studies motions of objects without taking the causes of these motions into account. Forward kinematics considers the relation between the configuration of the joints of a robotic arm and the position and orientation of the tip (or tool, hand, or end effector) of the arm. Inverse kinematics tackles the problem of configuring and controlling the joints of the arm in such a way that the tip can accomplish a given task. We also study motion or path planning, where the goal is to find a path for an autonomous robot from an initial to a final placement while avoiding collisions with the obstacles in its environment. We will learn how to translate the motion planning problem into a problem in so-called configuration space, and then study the structure of that space. We distinguish exact and approximate approaches to solving the problem. Exact approaches guarantee to find a path whenever one exists but are generally complex and only work for simple instances of the problem.
courseReview.contribution: Implements kinematics, manipulation, configuration-space motion planning and collision-free autonomous paths. It supplies computational robotics, not a claim to social-robot interaction or the VU embedded-systems engineering project.

courseReview.name: Introduction to Programming
courseReview.content: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
courseReview.contribution: establishes programming and computational problem solving

courseReview.name: Mathematical Methods
courseReview.content: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
courseReview.contribution: develops mathematical tools for computing

courseReview.name: Linear Algebra
courseReview.content: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.
courseReview.contribution: develops linear algebra for algorithms and machine learning

courseReview.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
courseReview.content: Many problems in science and engineering presented in a mathematical format do not have exact analyt- ical solutions; these problems can only be solved numerically. The nature of the mathematical problem dictates the type of numerical algorithm to use; solving an optimization problem requires a different al- gorithm than solving a differential equation. The prerequisite gateway courseMathematical Methods introduces techniques and methods for solving equations in one variable, for finding derivatives of func- tions, or for solving integrals,etc., analytically. This course focuses on the same mathematical concepts but from a numerical and computational perspective. Numerical solutions obtained through some al- gorithm pose the following challenge: what does the output mean? How sensitive is the algorithm to a wrong input? There are examples showing that numerical algorithms can produce completely wrong and unexpected outputs resulting in a disaster. Numerical and computational mathematics is a broad topic; numerous algorithms exist for numerically solving the same mathematical problem. This courses focuses on algorithms for solving equations in one variable. Several algorithms exist for interpolating or extrapolating functions on the basis of a set of sample points of that function. Numerical methods for differentiation, but especially integration form a set of very important numerical algorithms. The course discusses numerous algorithms for solving ordinary differential equations.
courseReview.contribution: uses computational numerical techniques to solve mathematical problems

courseReview.name: Advanced Calculus
courseReview.content: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.
courseReview.contribution: deepens calculus for computational modelling

courseReview.name: Linear Systems
courseReview.content: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.
courseReview.contribution: deepens linear systems methods for modelling

courseReview.name: Probability & Statistics
courseReview.content: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courseReview.contribution: develops probability and statistics for computing and data

courseReview.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courseReview.content: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives.
courseReview.contribution: Contributes epistemological questions, philosophical methods and precise argument about knowledge and claims; this supports critical evaluation of computational explanations, without supplying formal automata theory.

courseReview.name: Ethics
courseReview.content: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
courseReview.contribution: Examines moral theories and practical ethical arguments through papers and presentations, complementing AI Ethics with a wider foundation for responsible computing; it is not a CS thesis.

courseReview.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courseReview.content: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. courseReview.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courseReview.content: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. bioinformatics.actualContent: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).
